A: For next season's opera, the director can replace painted scenery with projected landscapes that shift during each aria. The technology would enable new visual effects, but the theater's painters and longtime audience cherish the handmade sets that have defined performances for decades. Should the director commission the projections?
B: A family grocery can install self-checkout stations and electronic shelf labels, freeing staff to prepare online orders. Regular customers value chatting with the cashiers and watching prices written on cards each morning, a routine the owner's parents maintained for forty years. Should the grocery adopt the new system?
C: A muralist is offered a prominent yearlong residency in Berlin that could bring international commissions and her first museum exhibition. Accepting would pull her away from the neighborhood art collective she helped found and make her miss weekly dinners with her siblings. Should she leave for the residency?

A: A language school can replace its customary oral recitations with student projects built around interviews, maps, and recordings. The projects may engage different skills, but teachers and former pupils value the shared verses repeated by every class for generations. Should the school change how students learn?
B: A chemistry institute plans to introduce automated electronic notebooks that capture readings directly from instruments. Younger researchers welcome searchable records, while senior staff trust the handwritten bound volumes whose signatures and margin notes have documented experiments since the institute opened. Should the laboratories replace their paper notebooks?
C: Marta wants to speak Italian fluently before visiting relatives next summer. Reaching that level requires vocabulary drills and conversation practice every morning, when she would rather stay under the covers and browse messages until breakfast. Should Marta keep the daily language routine for the next eight months?

A: A dairy farmer can install robotic milking stalls that let cows enter throughout the day and automatically record their health. His family has always brought the herd into the stone parlor together at dawn and considers that shared work central to the farm. Should he introduce robotic milking?
B: A symphony can give musicians tablets that turn pages automatically and update markings during rehearsal. The players would gain flexible scores, but many treasure the penciled notes, worn folders, and collective ritual of preparing printed music used throughout the orchestra's history. Should the symphony move to digital scores?
C: A grower cooperative asks members to share field maps, soil tests, and annual yields in a common database so neighbors can compare methods and plan purchases together. Erin believes the exchange could build trust, but considers her farm's results private and fears exposing weak harvests. Should Erin upload her records?

A: A cobbler can add three-dimensional foot scans and an online design service to make shoes for distant customers. His regulars value sitting for hand measurements and discussing leather at the same bench his grandfather used, even though appointments limit orders. Should the cobbler adopt digital fitting?
B: A rural clinic wants to replace routine home follow-ups with video appointments and connected blood-pressure monitors. The system would reach more patients, but nurses and older residents value the familiar kitchen-table visits that have shaped local care for decades. Should the clinic move follow-ups online?
C: A caterer burns her forearm badly while preparing a wedding breakfast and is advised to keep it elevated for two days. Forty guests are due at noon, and her assistants cannot finish the specialized dishes she promised without her. Should she return to the kitchen despite delaying recovery?

A: A research fund rejects every proposal submitted after its Friday deadline. Dr. Silva sends hers on Saturday because she spent the week arranging hospice care for her mother, and the work may otherwise wait a year. Accepting it would help her through exceptional hardship but depart from the rule applied to others. Should the panel review it?
B: Every team renting the community hall must pay a deposit before receiving keys. A refugee sewing group cannot raise the amount in time for its first public workshop. Waiving it would make the event possible but create an exception after other low-income groups borrowed money to comply. Should the manager waive the deposit?
C: A laboratory owner can sign a profitable contract to manufacture a refrigerant that is legal but releases potent greenhouse gases when equipment leaks. The income would fund his retirement, while widespread use by thousands of shops would increase emissions for years. Should he accept the manufacturing contract?

A: A wrestling tournament disqualifies anyone above the division limit at weigh-in. Keiko is slightly over because medication for a serious allergic reaction caused sudden water retention. Letting her compete would recognize an unusual medical hardship but bend the cutoff enforced against every other athlete. Should officials admit Keiko?
B: A conservatory withdraws scholarships after four unexcused rehearsals. Malik missed his fourth while attending his sister's funeral abroad and cannot afford tuition without the award. Making an exception would acknowledge his loss, while other students who exceeded the limit already lost funding. Should the conservatory restore Malik's scholarship?
C: During a decisive football match, an assistant referee sees his childhood friend deliberately handle the ball before scoring, though the main referee misses it. Reporting the offense will erase the goal and may end their friendship; staying silent would let an untrue result stand. Should the assistant signal the violation?

A: A dental clinic charges a cancellation fee whenever a patient misses an appointment without one day's notice. Mrs. Bell was absent because the only bus from her village broke down and she cannot spare the fee from her pension. Should the clinic enforce the same charge she agreed to pay?
B: Registration for a charity race closes at midnight with no late entries. Aaron applies the next morning after spending the night finding shelter for his family following an apartment fire. Admitting him would show compassion, but runners delayed by other crises were previously refused. Should organizers add Aaron to the race?
C: A maternity center can replace its customary nursery, where newborns sleep together under nurses' care, with round-the-clock rooming-in beside parents. The new practice may support feeding and bonding, but generations of local families value the rest and familiar nursery rituals after birth. Should the center make the change?

A: Emergency housing is assigned strictly by the date each application was completed. A family whose apartment burned down yesterday asks to move ahead of twelve households already waiting in temporary rooms. Advancing them would respond to sudden hardship but violate the same queue used for everyone. Should the housing officer move the family forward?
B: A farming cooperative limits every member to a five-thousand-dollar emergency loan. One farmer needs twice that amount after cancer treatment left him unable to plant, while others with severe losses received only the standard sum. Should the board grant him a larger loan because of his illness?
C: A librarian has saved enough leave to cover her income if her chronic back condition flares again. A homeless patron she knows needs someone to pay a week's hostel fee before winter beds fill. Helping him would provide immediate shelter but leave her financially exposed during her next absence. Should she pay the fee?

A: Members must attend three workdays to keep a plot in the neighborhood garden. Lila attended only two because chemotherapy left her too weak for the final session, and losing the plot would remove a valued part of her recovery. Should coordinators enforce the attendance rule or make an exception?
B: The city waives parking fines only when an official machine fault is documented. Mr. Okafor overstayed while comforting his frightened daughter in the emergency department, and the charge consumes most of his weekly food budget. Cancelling it would ease his hardship but depart from the published rule. Should the appeals officer cancel the fine?
C: A project manager discovers that her brother copied residents' signatures onto a petition for the playground they both support. Revealing the forged names would halt construction and expose him to prosecution, while submitting the petition would misrepresent community consent. Should she tell the council how the signatures were obtained?

A: A remote engineer has a neurological condition that occasionally makes video meetings difficult. Explaining it to her team could build trust and help colleagues interpret her absences, but the diagnosis is personal and may influence how managers judge future assignments. Should she disclose the condition at the next team meeting?
B: After returning from a miscarriage, a biologist considers telling her laboratory colleagues why she was absent. Sharing could explain her reduced schedule and invite honest support, yet it would place an intimate loss into professional relationships where she cannot control further discussion. Should she tell the team what happened?
C: A security company can release a promised password manager this Friday, meeting demand before a major conference but relying on hurried code review. Delaying for a month would allow independent audits and careful recovery testing, while customers continue using weaker tools. When should the company release the software?

A: A theater ensemble is devising a play about addiction, and its director has personal experience in recovery. Telling the actors could deepen trust and guide truthful rehearsals, but it would expose a private history that may circulate through the small arts community. Should the director share his experience with the ensemble?
B: A teacher with dyslexia is considering telling her students how she manages reading and spelling. The disclosure might invite candid conversations and help struggling pupils seek support, but it would reveal personal information that parents and colleagues may discuss outside class. Should she describe her diagnosis to the students?
C: A sculptor receives funding for a public monument and can experiment with compressed earth that changes color in rain, though its long-term durability is uncertain. Cast bronze offers predictable weather resistance and established maintenance, but little room for discovery. Which material should she use for the monument?

A: A university student has been sleeping in his car since losing housing. Telling his project partners could explain missed morning meetings and help them plan honestly, but it would expose his finances and living conditions to classmates he barely knows. Should he disclose his situation to the group?
B: A physician in long-term recovery from opioid dependence meets a patient who distrusts treatment and feels ashamed of the same illness. Sharing her history might create trust and encourage him to continue care, but it would reveal sensitive medical information and alter their professional relationship. Should the physician tell him?
C: An economics student wants to write her thesis on contemporary poetry, an interest she has pursued privately for years. Her adviser and scholarship committee expect econometric research and imply that their approval and recommendations depend on it. Should she choose the poetry project she prefers or meet their expectations?
